# Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger

This ledger records what the design guidance does not yet settle: hypotheses
resting on sparse evidence, version-sensitive mechanics, and tensions for
which either choice can fail. Its purpose is movement, not accumulation.
Questions graduate into doctrine when public documentation, source, tests, or
reproducible released-version probes support a bounded recommendation. They
retreat when counterexamples expose a missing condition, and the affected
doctrine should then be amended rather than silently defended.

Every entry should preserve the competing risks. More metadata can align
projections but make authoring and startup expensive. A richer semantic model
can enable analysis but duplicate a foreign authority. Strict admission can
protect invariants but destroy unknown content needed for round trips. The
ledger is useful only if it asks what evidence distinguishes those losses,
not merely whether a favored technique can be made to work.

## Scale of property metadata

[rtemis](07-ecosystem-field-guide.qmd#rtemis-property-contracts-as-inspectable-data)
shows contract-as-data driving validation, defaults, schema output, interfaces,
and contextual preparation. The unresolved question is when that machinery
pays for itself.

Evidence needed: maintenance histories comparing handwritten and
metadata-driven properties; contributor cost for adding or debugging a
property; alignment tests across releases; and examples where such a system
was simplified or removed.

## Promotion from reusable property to semantic class

A shared property names a contract cheaply; a class lets the value travel
independently and participate in dispatch. The boundary remains
judgment-dependent when a concept is meaningful but has no operation of its
own.

Evidence needed: cases where early promotion prevented ambiguity or rework;
cases where it only added wrapping overhead; and criteria based on extraction,
independent persistence, or operation vocabulary.

## Direct adaptation versus semantic IR

A pairwise adapter is simpler for one source and target. An IR may reduce
duplication across several sources and targets, but an “uber-schema” can merely
accumulate incidental fields.

Evidence needed: multiple real inputs or outputs sharing stable semantics;
operations that consume shared meaning independently of serialization;
preservation and loss matrices; and migration experience showing whether an IR
reduces or relocates complexity.

The competing risks are premature generalization and adapter proliferation.
An IR introduced before stable shared meaning is visible becomes another
schema to migrate. Waiting too long leaves every pairwise adapter to rediscover
normalization, equality, and loss policy. Graduation therefore requires
evidence from independent consumers, not the size of the class graph.

## Typed expression catalogs

Opaque expressions preserve engine authority and version flexibility. Typed
nodes enable analysis, safer construction, and multi-target compilation. The
point at which analysis justifies the catalog remains domain-specific.

Evidence needed: a substantive consumer beyond serialization; measured
versioning cost; a policy for unknown operators; and evidence that combinators
are insufficient but a full AST is maintainable.

## Deep value semantics with references

An S7 value may contain an environment, R6 object, external pointer,
connection, or cache. Replacing the outer value does not make referenced
internals independent, and inner mutation does not automatically re-run outer
validation.

Open questions include which payloads should be forbidden, snapshotted, or
excluded from equality and serialization; whether external memo tables keyed
by semantic content are reliable; and how APIs should state shallow versus
deep guarantees.

## Method coverage for open families

Abstract parents and fallback methods do not seal a family. Registries and
tests can check known variants, but extensions may add classes after those
checks run.

Open questions: whether coverage belongs at test time, registration, or first
use; how optional generics differ from missing methods; and how third parties
run reusable conformance suites. Native sealed-family or exhaustiveness
support would change the guidance.

## Explicit null, omission, and defaults

R's `NULL`, absent arguments, empty vectors, `NA`, and absent wire keys can
represent different states. Preserving every needed distinction remains
difficult, especially for generated constructors.

Evidence needed: released-version probes for omitted arguments versus explicit
`NULL`; public formats where omission changes behavior; ergonomic constructor
patterns; and serializer laws for omitted, `null`, empty, and defaulted states.

## Survival of unknown extensions

A pass-through bag promises fidelity only if every supported transformation
and serialization cycle preserves it. Typed and raw state can collide when a
specification promotes a formerly unknown field.

Open questions: whether extensions survive repeated read-modify-write cycles;
how upgrades detect collisions; whether preservation is byte-level,
structural, or normalized; and whether untrusted extensions create security
or resource risks. Corpus-based round-trip tests across released format
versions are needed.

## Persistence and class evolution

Persisted S7 values may outlive the package version that created them. Current
guidance prefers durable wire representations parsed by current code, but
compatibility policy is under-specified.

Open questions: explicit schema versions; migration registration and
composition; cross-release compatibility promises; serialized validator
environments; and S7 mechanics for revalidation after loading. Version-pinned
cross-release probes and public persistence policies are needed. RDS
compatibility should be stated narrowly rather than assumed.

## Equality relations

Exact `identical()` representation, canonical equality, domain equality, and
observational equivalence answer different questions. Packages often need
several, especially for reflected or normalized documents.

Open questions: which relation powers user comparison; whether canonicalization
is stored or computed; how extensions participate; and how diagnostics
suppress incidental noise.
[sqlr](07-ecosystem-field-guide.qmd#sqlr-one-model-for-rendering-reflection-and-comparison)
supplies one model; recurrence elsewhere would clarify reusable patterns.

## Strict parsing and tolerant admission

Strict known construction can coexist with a tolerant parser preserving
unknown or partial variants plus diagnostics. The unresolved issue is when
tolerance becomes unsafe or misleading.

Evidence needed: security boundaries requiring rejection; tools that preserve
partial documents but refuse compilation; policies for diagnostics and
revalidation; and issue histories showing whether partial values clarify or
defer failures.

## Aggregate-root granularity

Deep documents resist a simple “one document, one validator” rule. A single
root can enforce cross-reference invariants in one place, but it also makes a
small edit pay for traversal of an entire graph and can turn unrelated
subtrees into one consistency boundary. Nested roots localize construction,
replacement, and diagnostics, but delegation can miss invariants that cross
their boundaries or duplicate checks at several levels.

Evidence needed: real document models with cross-references at multiple
depths; mutation traces showing which edits require global knowledge; failure
reports comparing one root with delegated roots; and examples where aggregate
boundaries remained stable as the format evolved. The question should
graduate only as a decision rule for choosing a boundary, not as a fixed
maximum tree depth.

## Diagnostic duplication threshold

The guidance permits a cheap, documented duplicate check when it catches a
bad input at a boundary with a materially better message. “Cheap” remains
undefined. One duplicate can improve locality; several can drift, disagree on
edge cases, and obscure which rule is authoritative.

Evidence needed: maintenance histories where duplicate checks did or did not
drift; tests that prove equivalence to the authoritative rule; measurements
for checks on realistic payloads; and user evidence that the earlier
diagnostic changes recovery. A candidate threshold is that a duplicate must
have one named authority, an explicit equivalence test, negligible cost on
the boundary's expected payload, and no independent evolution. A duplicate
that needs its own exceptions or release policy has become a second authority
and should retreat.

## S7 version watch list

Recheck these mechanics against publication versions:

- constructor defaults and omitted versus explicit `NULL`;
- validator order, invocation count, and character-vector diagnostics;
- grouped replacement and deferred validation;
- getter output validation behavior;
- multiple dispatch specificity and `S7::super()`;
- environment, R6, and external-pointer properties;
- serialization across class-definition changes;
- package hooks relevant to validation or migration.

## Focused benchmark agenda

The useful question is not whether S7 is “fast.” Measurements should compare
design alternatives at the points where the guidance makes a choice, with R
and S7 versions, payload shape, garbage-collection policy, and warm-up stated.

**Bulk construction.** Compare constructor-per-node construction with
documented deferred-validation or batching mechanisms across realistic flat
and nested values. Record allocations and validation work as well as elapsed
time; a fast path that weakens the certification boundary is not equivalent.

**Grouped versus sequential replacement.** Compare `S7::set_props()` with
sequential `@<-` updates for several property counts and validator costs.
Measure intermediate copies and validator invocations, and include a case
where only the final grouped state is valid.

**Nested copy cost.** Vary top-level width, nesting depth, and shared payload
size to determine what replacement copies and what remains shared. Include
two-binding divergence checks so an optimization is not mistaken for a
semantic change.

**Hot-loop dispatch.** Compare direct calls, S3 dispatch, and S7 single and
multiple dispatch in representative compiler or tree-walk loops. Report the
fraction of total pass time attributable to dispatch; isolated nanoseconds do
not establish architectural significance.

**Metamodel startup.** Measure package load and class-definition cost as the
number and richness of property factories increase, including declaration
validation and generated projections. This tests the author-safety benefit
against interactive and worker-startup latency.

**Serialized-corpus overhead.** Compare many small S7 objects, aggregate
serialization, and durable wire forms across corpus sizes. Separate payload
bytes from repeated class or validator metadata, and test cross-version load
behavior rather than treating successful deserialization as compatibility.

These benchmarks should graduate guidance only when they reproduce across
released versions and realistic graphs. Surprising results should first
narrow the recommendation; they should not become a universal performance
claim.

## Evidence tripwires

Revise the guidance if S7 adds sealed classes, exhaustiveness checks, or
load-time migration; several packages sustain generated native graphs from
owned semantic specifications; property metadata is removed as uneconomic; a
typed AST is collapsed; an open bag beats a semantic model on long-term
correctness; or public round-trip corpora reveal systematic extension loss.

The ledger should also collect counterexamples: designs that violate current
defaults and work well, migrations away from S7 with stated reasons, and
duplicated checks that remain aligned because their diagnostic value is worth
the cost.

A counterexample entry should name the pressure the current guidance missed,
the competing risk that dominated, and the smallest exception that explains
the result. Repeated retreats are evidence that the doctrine's boundary is
wrong; an isolated exception is not permission to erase the boundary.
